copy.hook: All at once, or a little each month? 🪙

facts:
FINRA article 'The Benefits and Limitations of Dollar-Cost Averaging' (dated May 19, 2026), fetched 2026-11-25. Quotes:
"you invest your money in equal portions, at regular intervals, regardless of current market conditions";
"you'll buy more shares of an investment when the price is low and fewer shares when the price is high";
"can remove some of the emotion from investing"; "has lower risk but often produces lower returns than lump sum investing, especially over
longer periods of time"; "you could also miss out on some gains since part of your money stays in cash";
"If you pay commissions or other fees for each transaction, dollar-cost averaging might result in higher fees".
Both price series are made-up examples and the share counts are arithmetic: 100/10=10, 100/8=12.5, 100/12.5=8, sum 10+12.5+8+10=40.5,
400/40.5=9.88; 100/12.5=8, 100/20=5, 100/25=4, sum 10+8+5+4=27, 400/27=14.81; 400/10=40.
The publishing repository's file lessons.py is the lesson list of the live English app (its header: copied from the app's lessons, "44
lessons, the number on the App Store page", on 2026-10-20) and it contains "Dollar-Cost Averaging"; the published pipeline names lessons
from this list.

The publisher's records and SLE_CONTENT_LEDGER.md were read on 2026-11-25: this post was not published before. The owner asked for it to be prepared for the days before 2026-12-04.
slides_text:
SLIDE 1: All at once, or a little each month? Dollar-cost averaging, shown with two simple examples. All at once: $400. A little each month: $100 in months 1, 2, 3, 4.
SLIDE 2: Equal amounts, at regular intervals. As FINRA describes it, you split your money into same-size parts and invest them on a set schedule, in up and down markets alike. A fixed sum goes further when shares are cheap, and gets you fewer of them when they cost more. Lower price: $8 a share, 12.5 shares for $100. Higher price: $12.50 a share, 8 shares for $100.
SLIDE 3: Example 1. When the price moves down and up. Prices in months 1 to 4: $10, $8, $12.50, $10. $100 buys 10, 12.5, 8, 10 shares. $100 every month: 40.5 shares, average cost $9.88 a share. $400 in month 1: 40 shares, cost $10.00 a share. Here, buying monthly ends with slightly more shares. Fees are not included.
SLIDE 4: Example 2. When the price only goes up. Prices: $10, $12.50, $20, $25. $100 buys 10, 8, 5, 4 shares. $100 every month: 27 shares, average cost $14.81 a share. $400 in month 1: 40 shares, cost $10.00 a share. Here, all at once ends with more shares. Money waiting in cash can miss gains.
SLIDE 5: Three things to weigh. 1 Spreading purchases lowers risk, but often returns less than investing at once, especially over longer periods. 2 If you pay a fee on each purchase, more purchases can mean more fees. 3 A fixed schedule can take some of the emotion out of investing. Related lesson in the app: Dollar-Cost Averaging. Which would be easier for you to stick with? Tell us below.
FOOTER: Source: FINRA, The Benefits and Limitations of Dollar-Cost Averaging. Prices are made-up examples, not a real investment. Educational content only. Not financial or investment advice.
